title: Majestic Deception
reviewNotes: Five branches from seven pieces after Nxe8 at 82s. Bishop sacrifice leads to d8=N mate after Kxf7, or winning fxe8=Q after Kxg5. Independent dxe8=Q comparison draws; both careless queen-promotion mates checked. Earlier eight-piece rook sacrifice disclosed as context.
transcript: The queen is defending the promotion square. So, white is left with a rook and a bishop against a queen and a knight and is simply going to lose this game. Or at least you would think that. But after D7, we're attacking the black queen and trying to misplace it. The queen cannot take the pawn because we would promote with check and win. So, the black queen has to move to another square, but it has to be very careful. All of these squares are already defended by the white pieces. Going to B8 would allow a discovered check winning the queen. Going to D8 would allow bishop to G5 and after the black king moves, we would take the queen. And although the knight temporarily stops the promotion after bishop to E7, we are threatening two different promotions and we would win. And finally, after queen to A8, we would still have the brilliant bishop G5 check because after the king moves, we can now take the knight and we are again threatening two different promotions. So, the only move that seems to maintain the advantage for black is queen to F8, stepping in front of this pawn while also still defending the other promotion. [music] And now it seems like black is simply out of the woods and it's going to win this game, right? Well, not exactly because white has a majestic idea with the beautiful and brilliant move rook to E8. This is cutting the communication of the queen with the promotion square, threatening to get a new queen. But of course, the rook can simply be taken by the knight and it doesn't seem like white has achieved anything because we can't actually recapture this knight with either pawn. Although we promote, we are going to just get checkmated in one move. But white is not that naive and there was an idea behind this beautiful sacrifice. And that idea was to follow up with another sacrifice. Bishop to G5. But of course, if the king stops defending G7, there is going to be no mate threat. So, we would be able to promote. And once we escape a couple of checks, this is just going to be winning because white would get another queen. But wait a second, this is not checkers and black is not obligated to capture the bishop. Instead, the king can actually take one of the two pawns that we have left and still maintain the threat of a checkmate in one. Now promoting to a queen would just get us checkmated and taking the knight with a check would still land us in a completely lost end game. But there's no reason to panic because white had foreseen all of this and here he just promotes to a knight and delivers this beautiful knight and bishop checkmate.
